arXiv:math/0701394v2 [math.AP] 14 Jun 2007

Periodic solutions of forced Kirchhoff equations

Pietro Baldi Note: Sissa, via Beirut 2–4, 34014 Trieste, Italy. E-mail: baldi@sissa.it .
Abstract

We consider Kirchhoff equations for vibrating bodies in any dimension in presence of a time-periodic external forcing with period 2​π/ω2\pi/\omega and amplitude ε\varepsilon, both for Dirichlet and for space-periodic boundary conditions.

We prove existence, regularity and local uniqueness of time-periodic solutions of period 2​π/ω2\pi/\omega and order ε\varepsilon, by means of a Nash-Moser iteration scheme. The results hold for parameters (ω,ε)(\omega,\varepsilon) in Cantor sets having measure asymptotically full for ε→0\varepsilon\to 0. †† Keywords: Kirchhoff equation, periodic solutions, small divisors, Nash-Moser method. 2000 Mathematics Subjects Classification: 35L70; 45K05, 35B10, 37K55. Supported by MURST under the national project “Variational methods and nonlinear differential equations”.

1 Introduction

We consider the Kirchhoff equation

(1) ut​t−Δ​u​(1+∫Ω|∇u|2​𝑑x)=ε​g​(x,t)x∈Ω,t∈ℝu_{tt}-\Delta u\Big(1+\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}\,dx\Big)=\varepsilon g(x,t)\hskip 20.00003ptx\in\Omega,\ t\in{\mathbb{R}}

where gg is a time-periodic external forcing with period 2​π/ω2\pi/\omega and amplitude ε\varepsilon, and the displacement u:Ω×ℝ→ℝu:\Omega\times{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{R}} is the unknown. We consider both Dirichlet boundary conditions

(2) u⁡(x,t)=0∀x∈∂Ω,t∈ℝu(x,t)=0\hskip 10.00002pt\forall x\in\partial\Omega,\ t\in{\mathbb{R}}

where Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d} is a bounded, connected open set with smooth boundary, d≥1d\geq 1, and periodic boundary conditions on ℝd{\mathbb{R}}^{d}

(3) u⁡(x,t)=u⁡(x+2​π​m,t)∀m∈ℤd,x∈ℝd,t∈ℝu(x,t)=u(x+2\pi m,t)\hskip 10.00002pt\forall m\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{d},\ x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d},\ t\in{\mathbb{R}}

where Ω=(0,2​π)d\Omega=(0,2\pi)^{d}.

Equation (1) is a quasi-linear integro-partial differential equation having the structure of an infinite-dimensional Hamiltonian system, with time-depending Hamiltonian

H⁡(u,v)=∫Ωv22​𝑑x+∫Ω|∇u|22​𝑑x+(∫Ω|∇u|22​𝑑x)2−∫Ωε​g​u​𝑑x.H(u,v)=\int_{\Omega}\frac{v^{2}}{2}\,dx\,+\int_{\Omega}\frac{|\nabla u|^{2}}{2}\,dx\,+\Big(\int_{\Omega}\frac{|\nabla u|^{2}}{2}\,dx\Big)^{2}-\int_{\Omega}\varepsilon gu\,dx.

It describes nonlinear forced vibrations of a dd-dimensional body (in particular, a string for d=1d=1 and a membrane for d=2d=2).

This model has been proposed first in 1876 by Kirchhoff [23] in dimension one, without forcing terms, with Dirichlet boundary conditions, namely

(4) ut​t−ux​x​(1+∫0πux2​𝑑x)=0,u⁡(0,t)=u⁡(π,t)=0u_{tt}-u_{xx}\Big(1+\int_{0}^{\pi}u_{x}^{2}\,dx\Big)=0\,,\hskip 10.00002ptu(0,t)=u(\pi,t)=0

to describe transversal free vibrations of a clamped string in which the dependence of the tension on the deformation cannot be neglected. Independently, Carrier [14] and Narasimha [31] rediscovered the same equation as a nonlinear approximation of the exact model for the stretched string.

Kirchhoff equations have been studied by many authors from the point of view of the Cauchy problem

u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x),ut​(x,0)=u1​(x)u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)\,,\hskip 10.00002ptu_{t}(x,0)=u_{1}(x)

starting from the pioneering paper of Bernstein [6]. Both local and global existence has been investigated, for initial data having Sobolev or analytic regularity. See for example [18, 33, 26, 3, 17, 4, 28] and the rich surveys [2, 37].

In spite of the wide study for the Cauchy problem, to the best of our knowledge nothing is known about the existence of periodic solutions of Kirchhoff equations, except for the normal modes.

Kirchhoff himself observed that equation (4), thanks to its special symmetry, possesses a sequence of normal modes, that is solutions of the form u⁡(x,t)=uj​(t)​sin⁡j​xu(x,t)=u_{j}(t)\sin jx, j=1,2,…j=1,2,\ldots where uj​(t)u_{j}(t) is periodic. In general, normal modes are solutions of the form uj​(t)​φj​(x)u_{j}(t)\varphi_{j}(x) where φj​(x)\varphi_{j}(x) is an eigenfunction of the Laplacian on Ω\Omega.

In presence of a forcing term g⁡(x,t)g(x,t) this symmetry is broken and normal modes do not survive (except in the one-mode case g⁡(x,t)=gj​(t)​φj​(x)g(x,t)=g_{j}(t)\varphi_{j}(x)). Indeed, decomposing u⁡(x,t)=∑juj​(t)​φj​(x)u(x,t)=\sum_{j}u_{j}(t)\varphi_{j}(x) shows that all components uj​(t)u_{j}(t) are coupled in the integral term ∫Ω|∇u|2​𝑑x\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}dx, and problem (1) is equivalent to a system of infinitely many nonlinear coupled ODEs, namely

uj′′(t)+λj2uj(t)(1+∑kλk2uk2(t))=εgj(t),j=1,2,…u_{j}^{\prime\prime}(t)+\lambda_{j}^{2}u_{j}(t)\Big(1+\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}^{2}u_{k}^{2}(t)\Big)=\varepsilon g_{j}(t),\ \hskip 10.00002ptj=1,2,\ldots

where g⁡(x,t)=∑jgj​(t)​φj​(x)g(x,t)=\sum_{j}g_{j}(t)\varphi_{j}(x) and λj2\lambda_{j}^{2} are the eigenvalues of the Laplacian on Ω\Omega.

In this paper we prove the existence of periodic solutions of (1). We consider the amplitude ε\varepsilon and the frequency ω\omega of the forcing term gg as parameters of the problem. We prove that there exist periodic solutions of order ε\varepsilon and period 2​π/ω2\pi/\omega when ε\varepsilon is small and (ε,ω)(\varepsilon,\omega) belong to a Cantor set which has positive measure, asymptotically full for ε→0\varepsilon\to 0. We prove regularity estimates for the solutions, both in Sobolev and in analytic classes, and local uniqueness (see Theorem 1, Remark 1 and Theorem 2 in Section 2).

There are two main difficulties in looking for periodic solutions of (1). The first one is the so-called “small divisors problem”, caused by resonances between the forcing frequency ω\omega with its overtones and the eigenvalues λj2\lambda_{j}^{2} of the Laplacian on Ω\Omega. Such a problem arises in the inversion of the d’Alembert operator ∂t​t−Δ\partial_{tt}-\Delta, whose spectrum

{−ω2l2+λj2:l∈ℕ,j=1,2,…}\{-\omega^{2}l^{2}+\lambda_{j}^{2}\,:\,l\in{\mathbb{N}},\ j=1,2,\ldots\}

accumulates to zero for almost every ω\omega. For this reason, (∂t​t−Δ)−1(\partial_{tt}-\Delta)^{-1} cannot map, in general, a functional space in itself, but only in a larger space of less regular functions. This makes impossible the application of the standard implicit function theorem.

The other difficulty is the presence of derivatives in the nonlinearity. In general, little is known about periodic solutions of equations of the form

ut​t−ux​x=ε​f​(x,t,u,ux,ut,ux​x,ux​t,ut​t).u_{tt}-u_{xx}=\varepsilon f(x,t,u,u_{x},u_{t},u_{xx},u_{xt},u_{tt}).

This problem has been studied by Rabinowitz [35] in presence of a dissipative term α​ut\alpha u_{t}, α≠0\alpha\neq 0, and frequency ω=1\omega=1; by Craig [15] for pseudodifferential operators

ut​t−ux​x=a(x)u+b(x,|∂x|βu)=0,β<1;u_{tt}-u_{xx}=a(x)u+b(x,|\partial_{x}|^{\beta}u)=0\,,\hskip 10.00002pt\beta<1\,;

by Bourgain [13] in cases like ut​t−ux​x+ρ​u+ut2=0u_{tt}-u_{xx}+\rho u+u_{t}^{2}=0 and, for quasiperiodic solutions, [10] ut​t−ux​x=a⁡(x)​u+ε​∂x1/2(h⁡(x,u))u_{tt}-u_{xx}=a(x)u+\varepsilon\partial_{x}^{1/2}(h(x,u)). We remark that, in general, the presence of derivatives in the nonlinearity makes uncertain the existence of global (even not periodic) solutions, see for example the non-existence results in [21, 24] for the equation ut​t−a⁡(ux)​ux​x=0u_{tt}-a(u_{x})u_{xx}=0 when a>0a>0, a⁡(v)=O⁡(vp)a(v)=O(v^{p}) near 00, p≥1p\geq 1.

Our proof overcomes these two difficulties by means of a modified Newton’s method in scales of Banach spaces, that is a Nash-Moser method. At each step of the Newton’s iteration we impose some “non-resonance conditions” on the parameter ω\omega to control small divisors. For these non-resonance frequencies we can invert the linearised operator, which is a perturbation of the d’Alembertian, losing some amount of regularity. In this way we construct inductively a sequence of approximate solutions. The loss of regularity, which occurs at each step of the iteration, is overcome thanks to smoothing operators and to the high speed of convergence of the quadratic scheme.

The application of Nash-Moser methods to infinite-dimensional dynamical systems having small divisors problems has been introduced in the Nineties by Craig, Wayne and Bourgain, in analytic or Gevray classes [16, 12, 13, 15]. Further developments are for example in [9, 5, 7, 32].

This technique, combined with Lyapunov-Schmidt reductions, is a flexible alternative with respect to KAM procedures [38, 25, 34]. In particular, currently available KAM methods seem not to apply to the quasi-linear problem (1).

Since we deal with not only analytic, but also finite order regularity, the scheme we use here differs from that in [9, 5] and it does not rely on analyticity assumptions. Such a procedure goes back directly to ideas of the original methods of [29, 30, 39] and it is developed in [7]. Recently [8] this technique has made possible to prove the existence of periodic solutions of nonlinear wave equations for nonlinearities having only CkC^{k} differentiability. We point out that some of the difficulties of [8] are not present here, thanks to the special symmetry of the Kirchhoff nonlinearity. Moreover, the roles played here by space and time are inverted with respect to [8, 9, 5].

We remark that small divisors problems become more difficult in higher dimension. For this reason, not many works deal with such problems when the dimension is larger than one (e.g. [11, 12]). In that case, indeed, λj\lambda_{j} have a sub-linear growth, see (6). In general this causes further difficulties in the inversion of the linearised operators. In the present case, however, the structure of the Kirchhoff nonlinear integral term makes possible the inversion in any dimension (Section 6).

Finally, we note that in case of periodic boundary conditions (3) zero is an eigenvalue of the Laplacian. As a consequence, we have to solve a space-average equation which is not present in the Dirichlet case (2), see (57) in Section 7.

2 Functional setting and main results

Let 2​π/ω2\pi/\omega be the period of gg. We look for solutions uu with the same period. Normalising the time t→ω​tt\to\omega t and rescaling u→ε1/3​uu\to\varepsilon^{1/3}u, (1) becomes

(5) ω2​ut​t−Δ​u=μ⁡(Δ​u​∫Ω|∇u|2​𝑑x+g⁡(x,t))\omega^{2}u_{tt}-\Delta u=\mu\Big(\Delta u\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}\,dx+g(x,t)\Big)

where μ:=ε2/3\mu:=\varepsilon^{2/3} and g,ug,u are 2​π2\pi-periodic.

with ∫Ωφj2​𝑑x=1\int_{\Omega}\varphi_{j}^{2}\,dx=1 and λ1<λ2≤…\lambda_{1}<\lambda_{2}\leq\ldots . Weyl’s formula for the asymptotic distribution of the eigenvalues gives λj=O⁡(j1/d)\lambda_{j}=O(j^{1/d}) as j→∞j\to\infty, thus

(Case of Dirichlet boundary conditions). Suppose that g∈Xσ,s0g\in X_{\sigma,s_{0}} for some σ≥0\sigma\geq 0, s0>2​ds_{0}>2d. Let s1∈(1+d,1+s0/2)s_{1}\in(1+d,1+s_{0}/2). There exist positive constants δ,C\delta,C with the following properties.

2.2 Case of periodic boundary conditions

The eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the Laplacian on 𝕋d{\mathbb{T}}^{d} are |m|2|m|^{2}, ei​m⋅xe^{im\cdot x} for m∈ℤdm\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}. We consider a bijective numbering {mj:j∈ℕ}\{m_{j}:j\in{\mathbb{N}}\} of ℤd{\mathbb{Z}}^{d} such that |mj|≤|mj+1||m_{j}|\leq|m_{j+1}| for all j∈ℕ={0,1,…}j\in{\mathbb{N}}=\{0,1,\ldots\}, and we denote

λ~j2:=|mj|2,φ~j​(x):=ei​mj⋅x∀j∈ℕ.\tilde{\lambda}_{j}^{2}:=|m_{j}|^{2},\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{\varphi}_{j}(x):=e^{im_{j}\cdot x}\hskip 10.00002pt\ \forall j\in{\mathbb{N}}.

X~σ,s:={u(x,t)=∑j≥0uj(t)φ~j(x):uj∈H1(𝕋,ℝ),∥u∥σ,s2:=∥u0∥H12+∑j≥1∥uj∥H12λ~j2​se2​σ​λ~j<∞}.\tilde{X}_{\sigma,s}:=\Big\{u(x,t)=\sum_{j\geq 0}u_{j}(t)\tilde{\varphi}_{j}(x):\,u_{j}\in H^{1}({\mathbb{T}},{\mathbb{R}}),\\ \|u\|_{\sigma,s}^{2}:=\|u_{0}\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\sum_{j\geq 1}\|u_{j}\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\tilde{\lambda}_{j}^{2s}\,e^{2\sigma\tilde{\lambda}_{j}}<\infty\Big\}.
Theorem 2.

(Case of periodic boundary conditions). Suppose that g∈X~σ,s0g\in\tilde{X}_{\sigma,s_{0}} for some σ≥0\sigma\geq 0, s0>2​ds_{0}>2d, and

(8) ∫(0,2​π)d+1g⁡(x,t)​𝑑x​𝑑t=0.\int_{(0,2\pi)^{d+1}}g(x,t)\,dxdt=0\,.

Let s1∈(1+d,1+s0/2)s_{1}\in(1+d,1+s_{0}/2). There exist positive constants δ,C\delta,C with the following properties.

For every γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1) there exists a Cantor set 𝒜γ⊂(0,+∞)×(0,δ​γ)\mathcal{A}_{\gamma}\subset(0,+\infty)\times(0,\delta\gamma) of parameters such that for every (ω,μ)∈𝒜γ(\omega,\mu)\in\mathcal{A}_{\gamma} there exists a classical solution u⁡(ω,μ)∈X~σ,s1u(\omega,\mu)\in\tilde{X}_{\sigma,s_{1}} of (5)(3) satisfying

∫(0,2​π)d+1u⁡(ω,μ)​(x,t)​𝑑x​𝑑t=0.\int_{(0,2\pi)^{d+1}}u(\omega,\mu)(x,t)\,dxdt=0\,.

Such a solution satisfies

(9) ‖u⁡(ω,μ)‖σ,s1≤μγ​(1+1ω2)​C,‖u​(ω,μ)t​t‖σ,s1−2≤μγ​ω2​C\|u(\omega,\mu)\|_{\sigma,s_{1}}\leq\frac{\mu}{\gamma}\,\Big(1+\frac{1}{\omega^{2}}\Big)\,C\,,\hskip 20.00003pt\|u(\omega,\mu)_{tt}\|_{\sigma,s_{1}-2}\leq\frac{\mu}{\gamma\omega^{2}}\,C

and it is unique in the ball {∫(0,2​π)d+1u(x,t)dxdt=0,∥u∥σ,s1<1}\{\int_{(0,2\pi)^{d+1}}u(x,t)\,dxdt=0,\ \|u\|_{\sigma,s_{1}}<1\}.

The set 𝒜γ\mathcal{A}_{\gamma} satisfies the same measure property of Theorem 1.

Remark 4.

If u⁡(ω,μ)u(\omega,\mu) is a solution of (5)(3), then also u⁡(ω,μ)+cu(\omega,\mu)+c, c∈ℝc\in{\mathbb{R}}, solves (5)(3).

2.3 Outline of the proof

The rest of the paper is devoted to the proof of the theorems. In Sections 3,4,5,6 we develop the details for the proof of Theorem 1, then the same calculations are used to prove Theorem 2 in Section 7.

In Section 3 we perform the Nash-Moser iteration to construct the approximating sequence (un)(u_{n}), for μ\mu small and (ω,μ)(\omega,\mu) belonging to smaller and smaller “non-resonant” sets AnA_{n}. Avoiding resonances allows to invert the linearised operator at each step of the iteration.

In Section 4 we prove that unu_{n} converges to a solution of the Kirchhoff equation if (ω,μ)∈An(\omega,\mu)\in A_{n} for all nn. Local uniqueness of the solution is also proved.

In Section 5 we prove that the intersection of all AnA_{n} is a nonempty set, which is very large in a Lebesgue measure sense.

In Section 6 we prove the invertibility of the linearised operator for (ω,μ)∈An(\omega,\mu)\in A_{n} and we give an estimate on the inverse operator.

In Section 7 we complete the proof of Theorem 1 and we prove Theorem 2.

6 Inversion of the linearised operator

In this section we prove Lemma 1. Let u∈X(n),h∈X(n+1)u\in X^{(n)},h\in X^{(n+1)}. The linearised operator is

F′​(u)​h=Lω​h−μ​f′​(u)​[h]=D​h+S​h\displaystyle F^{\prime}(u)h=L_{\omega}h-\mu f^{\prime}(u)[h]=Dh+Sh

where we split F′​(u)F^{\prime}(u) in a diagonal part

D​h:=ω2​ht​t−Δ​h​(1+μ​∫Ω|∇u|2​𝑑x)Dh:=\omega^{2}h_{tt}-\Delta h\Big(1+\mu\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}\,dx\Big)

and a “projection” part

Sh:=−μΔu∫Ω2∇u∘∇hdx.Sh:=-\mu\Delta u\int_{\Omega}2\nabla u\circ\nabla h\,dx\,.

We recall here some results on Hill’s problems. The proof is in the Appendix.

Lemma 7.

(Hill’s problems). Let α⁡(t)\alpha(t) be 2​π2\pi-periodic and ‖α‖∞<1/2\|\alpha\|_{\infty}<1/2. The eigenvalues p2p^{2} of the periodic problem

(50) {y′′+p2​(1+α⁡(t))​y=0y⁡(t)=y⁡(t+2​π)\begin{cases}y^{\prime\prime}+p^{2}(1+\alpha(t))\,y=0\\ y(t)=y(t+2\pi)\end{cases}

form a sequence {pl2}l∈ℕ\{p_{l}^{2}\}_{l\in{\mathbb{N}}} such that

(51) 13​l≤pl≤2​l∀l∈ℕ.\frac{1}{3}\,l\leq p_{l}\leq 2l\hskip 10.00002pt\,\forall l\in{\mathbb{N}}.

For α,β\alpha,\beta 2​π2\pi-periodic, ‖α‖∞,‖β‖∞<1/2\|\alpha\|_{\infty},\|\beta\|_{\infty}<1/2,

(52) |pl​(α)−pl​(β)|≤2​l​‖α−β‖∞∀l∈ℕ.\big|p_{l}(\alpha)-p_{l}(\beta)\big|\leq 2l\,\|\alpha-\beta\|_{\infty}\hskip 10.00002pt\,\forall l\in{\mathbb{N}}.

The eigenfunctions ψl​(t)\psi_{l}(t) of (50) form an orthonormal basis of L2​(𝕋)L^{2}({\mathbb{T}}) w.r.t. the scalar product

(u,v)Lα2=∫02​πu​v​(1+α)​𝑑t(u,v)_{L^{2}_{\alpha}}=\int_{0}^{2\pi}uv(1+\alpha)\,dt

and also an orthogonal basis of H1​(𝕋)H^{1}({\mathbb{T}}) w.r.t. the scalar product

Proof of Theorem 1. Let g∈Xσ,s0g\in X_{\sigma,s_{0}} and 2​d<2​(s1−1)<s02d<2(s_{1}-1)<s_{0} as assumed in the theorem. We apply Lemma 2 with

τ:=s1−1.\tau:=s_{1}-1\,.
